context: A research team is preparing a governance analysis of AI systems and must decide which systems fall within its scope. The field includes a wide spectrum of systems, from the largest, most capable general-purpose models down to small, narrowly specialized tools. A narrow scope would concentrate attention on the systems with the greatest potential for broad impact and the most novel risks. A wider scope would capture the full range of deployed systems and align with a general functional notion of what counts as an AI system, but would stretch the analysis across very different technologies and risk profiles. The team must fix the boundary of coverage before beginning the analysis.
a_text: Define coverage by a broad functional definition of AI systems and include any autonomous machine-based system that infers outputs, whatever its size.
b_text: Restrict coverage to highly advanced, broadly capable frontier AI systems and exclude small or specialized systems from the analysis.
reason: Narrow systems are less likely to pose severe risks when deployed internally. A targeted focus allows tailored interventions justified by national security and societal concerns without unduly hindering innovation.

context: A research team is preparing a review that draws lessons from existing safety-critical industries to inform how risks from a new technology should be governed. Many industries could serve as analogues, including those handling biological agents and toxins, novel chemical substances, novel pesticides, nuclear reactor research and development, and experimental aircraft. The team cannot cover all of them in equal depth within the main body of the review and must decide which industries to treat as the central analogues and which to give secondary treatment, such as placing them in an appendix. The choice shapes which regulatory practices, risk-assessment approaches and lessons the review emphasizes.
a_text: Focus the main review on biological agents and toxins, novel chemical substances and novel pesticides, and move nuclear reactor R&D and experimental aircraft to the appendix.
b_text: Focus the main review on nuclear reactor R&D and experimental aircraft, and move biological agents and toxins, novel chemicals and novel pesticides to the appendix.
reason: These industries have the most similar threat profile: high impact, wide reach, high velocity and difficult to remediate. They also allow regulated pre-release access and use.

context: A research team is analysing whether existing legal and regulatory frameworks for AI govern internal deployment, meaning use of advanced AI systems inside the developing organisation without public release. These frameworks were mostly written with external, market-facing release in mind, and their text does not address internal use explicitly. The team must decide how strongly to state the conclusion about coverage in its analysis. A firm claim would give policymakers and regulators a clear position, but it could be challenged as overreaching. A more qualified claim would be easier to defend, but it could weaken the practical force of the finding.
a_text: State that the frameworks can be interpreted to cover internal deployment while explicitly declining to advocate an extensive or creative reading.
b_text: State that the existing guidance covers internal deployment by defining a deployer as any organisation using an AI system internally or externally.
reason: The review is only of how the language could in theory be read, not a recommendation that it should be.

context: A legal analysis addresses the scope of a regulation on artificial intelligence. One operative article states that the regulation applies to AI systems put into service for the deployer's own use, which would cover systems built and used internally by an organisation. A recital in the same regulation states that systems developed and put into service for the purpose of scientific research and development fall outside the regulation. Read broadly, the recital could remove internally deployed research and development systems from scope, which would conflict with the operative article. Recitals are interpretive aids and are not themselves binding rules. The analysis must decide how the recital relates to the operative article when applied to internally deployed systems.
a_text: Treat the recital as a narrow exception to the operative article, so that systems with the sole purpose of scientific research and development fall outside the scope.
b_text: Treat the recital as creating no exception to the operative article, so that AI systems put into service for own use stay within the regulation's scope.
reason: Recitals have no binding legal force and cannot derogate from the Act's actual provisions, according to EU Court of Justice case law.

context: A research team is writing a paper that analyses how safety-critical industries are governed, in order to draw lessons for the oversight of frontier AI. They have material on two industries: aviation, including experimental aircraft development, and nuclear power, including test reactors. They must decide how to structure the paper. The case studies could either be placed in the main text, where they would shape the central argument and serve as the comparison industries for governance lessons, or be moved to a supplementary appendix, leaving the main text to focus on other material. The choice affects how prominent these two industries are in the paper's framing and how much of the argument rests on them.
a_text: Move the experimental aircraft and test nuclear reactor case studies to the appendix and keep them out of the main text.
b_text: Keep the aviation and nuclear power case studies in the main text as the two core comparison industries for drawing governance lessons.
reason: Aviation and nuclear threats are more localized and may lack the high impact, wide reach, velocity and difficulty of remediation shared by AI, biological agents, chemicals and pesticides.

context: A team is deciding how to learn the risk profile of an advanced AI system before it is deployed internally within the developing organisation. Internal deployment can give the system access to sensitive resources and its own developers' workflows, so problems discovered only after deployment could be costly. The team must choose between a gating approach that relies on evaluations run on a nearly finished system and an approach that moves risk assessment earlier in development.
a_text: Require scheming and control evaluations on the system before internal deployment, and make deployment conditional on passing results.
b_text: Test for dangerous capabilities early in development and forecast future models' capabilities, so that models posing unacceptable risks are never built.
reason: Scheming is a horizontal risk layer that can undermine all other evaluations, so it must be assessed before the first highly capable systems are applied to AI R&D.

context: A team is designing governance recommendations for how organisations should handle information about AI systems they deploy internally for their own operations. Such systems can affect staff and decisions made within the organisation, and oversight bodies such as government regulators have a legitimate interest in them. The team has already settled that staff and government should receive substantial information about these systems. The open question is how much to disclose to the general public in comparison. Public disclosure could support accountability, trust and the ability of affected people to challenge decisions, but it also carries costs: the effort of maintaining detailed records, possible exposure of sensitive operational or security details, and the risk of inconsistent reporting across organisations. The team must choose the level of public disclosure to recommend.
a_text: Require detailed public disclosure of each deployed AI tool through a standardized public register covering its status, purpose, human role, and appeal mechanisms.
b_text: Recommend minimal, high-level public disclosure, such as the existence of governance frameworks, instead of detailed information about individual systems.
reason: Detailed public information could fuel race dynamics, while the public still benefits from a high-level outline given the potential spill of threats into society.

context: A team is designing a framework for reviewing whether an organisation's governance mechanisms work in practice. One component under consideration is whistleblower channels, which let insiders report suspected wrongdoing and are widely cited as an important route by which fraud is uncovered. The team must decide how much weight to place on these channels when judging governance effectiveness. A heavy reliance would make the volume of reports received a headline indicator, while a lighter reliance would treat the channels as one contributor among several. The team is aware that report counts can reflect trust in the channel, workforce size, or underlying misconduct, and that the channels depend on protections and on people being willing to use them.
a_text: Adopt the number of whistleblower reports received as a core effectiveness measure because tips account for a large share of fraud detection.
b_text: Describe whistleblower channels and protections as a useful aid that must not serve as the only mechanism for reviewing governance effectiveness.
reason: Whistleblower channels support review of whether mechanisms function and suffice as capabilities grow, but are not sufficient alone.

context: A research team is designing an automated monitor that reviews the outputs or actions of an AI system and must communicate its judgment to downstream users or systems. The monitor is an LLM-based judge, and the team must decide the format of its output. A simple format would have it return a single verdict that either blocks or approves each item. Different deployments are likely to tolerate different levels of risk and different false-positive and false-negative costs, and a single fixed judgment may not suit all of them. A judge asked to give one overall verdict may also fold several distinct considerations into one opaque decision, which makes its reasoning harder to inspect and verify. The team must choose how the monitor structures its output.
a_text: Have the judge evaluate each requirement of the response separately and cite supporting evidence for each judgment instead of returning one overall score or verdict.
b_text: Have the monitor output a graded severity score and let users set their own blocking threshold instead of returning a binary block or approve decision.
reason: Risk tolerance varies across users, e.g. a bank wants stronger guarantees than a personal website builder

context: A team building a monitor that flags unsafe behavior by AI agents needs to measure how faithfully the monitor detects such behavior, which it calls fidelity. Real examples of attacks or failures in deployment are scarce, so the team cannot rely on naturally occurring data to estimate detection performance. The team must choose a way to produce attack data for evaluating the monitor, and the choice determines how realistic the test cases are and how much control the team has over their characteristics.
a_text: Inject specified failure modes at specified severities into real agent trajectories to build synthetic attacks, and measure how often the monitor catches them.
b_text: Run an attacker model that is instructed to attempt attacks inside simulated copies of the real deployment environment, and measure how often the monitor catches them.
reason: Real data has higher complexity and attack surface, traditional settings likely underestimate real-world attack rates, and injections allow specificity about failure modes

context: A team is designing a real-time monitor that can block or interrupt an automated agent's actions before they complete, alongside slower monitors that review work later, such as at pull-request level or in delayed batch analysis. Blocking is costly: it interrupts workflows, so the monitor's scope must be limited. The team must decide which failure modes the real-time blocking monitor should cover and which should be left to the slower monitors. Failure modes range from harms that are immediate and hard to reverse to risks that are only potential and can be caught and fixed afterward. The team must set the principle that determines what qualifies for real-time blocking.
a_text: Limit the real-time monitor's threat model to risks where harm is instantaneous and hard to recover from, such as data exfiltration, and leave risks that later review can catch to slower monitors.
b_text: Define urgent, interrupt-worthy alerts by user-facing symptoms rather than underlying causes, and route merely risky conditions that could harm users later to lower-urgency tickets handled the next day.
reason: Real-time blocking is needed only where harm is instantaneous and hard to reverse; delayed monitoring allows more capable models for the other risks

context: A research team is building a monitoring pipeline in which a monitor model reviews the behavior of an AI system and flags problematic actions. Each flagged item needs a severity level so that results can be compared, aggregated, and acted on. The team must decide how that severity is assigned. One approach is a predefined deterministic rule set that maps observable features of the behavior to severity levels. This would be transparent and reproducible, but it may miss nuance. The other approach is to let the monitor model weigh the surrounding context and decide severity case by case. This would be more flexible and sensitive to circumstances, but it would be less predictable and harder to audit.
a_text: Assign severity through the monitor model's contextual judgment of each case instead of fixed rules.
b_text: Assign severity with a fixed deterministic rule set that maps observed behaviors to severity levels.
reason: Deployments are too varied for a clean rule set; the same command can be benign or malicious depending on context; also Watcher improves as model judgment improves

context: A research team runs an automated monitoring system in which a language model repeatedly reviews the steps of a long multi-step agent trajectory. Each call sends the same large system prompt plus the accumulating history of earlier steps, so token cost grows quickly with trajectory length. The team wants to lower this cost without noticeably harming monitoring quality. Two broad levers are available: keep the detailed prompts and depend on provider-side prompt caching to make repeated prefixes cheaper, or reduce the number of tokens sent by rewriting the prompt more compactly and condensing the earlier history. The detailed prompts currently work well, and caching discounts apply only to unchanged repeated prefixes, while compression risks losing information the monitor needs.
a_text: Keep the long, detailed monitoring prompts unchanged and rely on prompt caching to offset the repeated cost.
b_text: Compress the repeated system prompt into compact shorthand and have a cheaper model condense earlier steps into a brief summary.
reason: All compactions reduced performance, and caching makes the overhead of long prompts nearly negligible

context: A research team built a pipeline that uses language models to generate synthetic severity labels for steps in simulated attack sequences, and plans to use these labels as the basis for evaluating other systems. Before relying on them, the team must establish whether the labels are trustworthy. The labels come from an automated rubric-based process, and the team knows that LLM-based judgments can carry biases such as favoring longer outputs or outputs resembling the judge's own style. Edge cases in the rubric may produce inconsistent labels. The team has limited annotation resources and must choose how to verify label quality before using them for evaluation.
a_text: Skip human annotation and validate the labels by running two independent LLM judges, calibrated for known biases, and keep only the labels on which both agree.
b_text: Validate the labels against a human-annotated reference set of attack steps, refining the rubric wherever edge cases cause inconsistencies, and use the resulting set for evaluation.
reason: Otherwise the datasets would be miscalibrated and the evaluation misleading

context: A research team is building a monitor, itself a model, that reviews the behavior of an AI agent acting over multi-step tasks and flags suspicious or unsafe actions. The agent's trajectory contains several message types: the task instructions, the agent's reasoning and messages, the tool calls it makes, and the outputs those tools return. Tool outputs can be very long and noisy, and they may carry information that helps or misleads the monitor. The team must decide how much of the trajectory, and which message types, the monitor sees when it scores each trajectory. The choice affects the monitor's detection accuracy, its cost, and how much it can be influenced by content in the tool outputs.
a_text: Show the monitor the full conversation context with all tool call outputs included.
b_text: Show the monitor the full conversation context with all tool call outputs removed.
reason: More context improves performance, but tool outputs hold most tokens, so removing them greatly lowers cost and latency at slight fidelity loss

context: A team is building a multi-model agent tool and must decide how its Default configuration selects models. Several frontier models of differing capability and cost are available. One design is an automatic cascade: a cheap triage model scores each task, and a numeric threshold decides whether the task is escalated to a stronger gateway model. A lighter configuration could reuse this cascade with a higher threshold and a cheaper gateway model. The alternative design avoids automatic routing: the Default fixes one strong model at high reasoning effort, and any delegation to other models is left to written guidance that the model reads. The team must choose which design the Default uses, knowing that the cascade adds tunable parameters and moving parts, while the fixed model is simpler but gives up automatic cost and capability matching.
a_text: Configure Default with one fixed strong model at high reasoning effort, and leave delegation to other models to written guidance rather than an automatic triage cascade..
b_text: Configure Default as an automatic cascade, with a cheap triage model escalating tasks at a set threshold to a stronger gateway model, and a Lite variant using a higher threshold and cheaper gateway.
reason: Luna is cheap, fast and errs on the side of escalating; Opus 4.7 offers the best mix of fidelity, cost and latency at threshold 6; Sonnet is a lower-cost alternative

context: A research team is developing and optimizing attacks against automated monitoring systems for AI agents. They have access to two existing evaluation sets: a suite of agentic sabotage tasks, each pairing a main task with a hidden side task, and a set of alignment-faking test cases. The team needs to decide how these sets fit into the project timeline. Using the full sets throughout development risks overfitting the attacks to the evaluation data, while reserving them leaves less real data available during optimization. The team must choose how to allocate these datasets between attack development and final evaluation.
a_text: Hold the full sabotage and alignment-faking datasets out of sample and reserve them for evaluation until later in the project.
b_text: Evaluate on a selected subset of nine sabotage task pairs and optimize the attacks on separately generated synthetic data.
reason: Keeping them out of sample preserves them for later generalisation testing.

context: A research team is building and tuning monitors, which are classifiers that flag suspicious behavior, and runs a grid search over monitor configurations to select the best one. Each configuration must be scored by a single metric so that candidates can be ranked. Monitors are evaluated across several subcategories of behavior, and a deployable monitor eventually needs a decision threshold for flagging. The team must decide how to score candidates during the search. One approach ties the score to a threshold-dependent measure, with the threshold recomputed separately for each monitor subcategory. The other approach uses a threshold-independent ranking measure for selection and leaves the threshold unset until a monitor has been chosen.
a_text: Score each candidate monitor with a threshold-dependent metric, recomputing the threshold separately for every monitor subcategory during the grid search.
b_text: Score each candidate monitor with a threshold-independent ranking metric during the grid search, and set the threshold only after a monitor is selected.
reason: AUROC is threshold agnostic, and per-monitor threshold recomputation would be cumbersome.

context: A research team is building and evaluating a system on a labeled dataset in which some labels are suspected to be incorrect. They use LLM-based assistants as monitors that review examples and flag labels they judge to be wrong. Acting on these flags by relabeling would improve the accuracy of the labels. However, because the monitors themselves are the source of the corrections, relabeling based on their judgments introduces bias into evaluation, since the evaluation metric would then favor outputs that agree with the monitors. The team must decide whether to allow this relabeling or to keep the labels fixed so that the evaluation metric stays fair and unbiased.
a_text: Keep the labels fixed and never relabel from monitor flags, so the evaluation metric stays fair and unbiased.
b_text: Relabel whenever a monitor convincingly flags a label as wrong, accepting biased evaluation in exchange for more accurate labels.
reason: Their primary goal is to build the best possible monitor, not to preserve an unbiased metric. They also expect the bias to be acceptably small.

context: A team has developed a language model that produces an extended internal chain of thought before giving its final answer. They must decide what to advise about whether this chain of thought should be shown to end users. Showing it could help users trust the model, check its answers, and prompt it more effectively. It could also expose unfiltered, unpolished reasoning, and the team has limited evidence about how users would respond to it in practice. The team must choose between giving a clear recommendation on visibility and leaving the question open.
a_text: Recommend showing the model's raw chain of thought to users, on the grounds that it builds trust and helps them verify answers and get better outputs.
b_text: Withhold any recommendation on showing the model's raw chain of thought to users, and leave the question of its visibility open.
reason: Visibility could backfire by creating pressure to directly supervise the CoT to look safe and to avoid legal and reputational risks, which may break monitorability.

context: A research team is writing about chain-of-thought monitoring as a safety tool for advanced reasoning models. Their argument depends on the externalized reasoning property: the idea that, for hard tasks, a model's chain of thought must contain the reasoning needed to reach its answer and so reflects what drives its behavior. They must decide how strongly to claim that today's reasoning models satisfy this property. Prior evidence is mixed. Chains of thought often look informative, but it is unclear whether they always acknowledge the factors that influence a model's answer, and the property may weaken in future models. The team can either state a position about current models or gather direct evidence on them.
a_text: State a hedged belief that current models satisfy the property, and note that this does not guarantee monitorability and may fail for future models.
b_text: Measure across several reasoning models how often chains of thought acknowledge hints embedded in prompts, and treat faithfulness as a property to test rather than assume.
reason: Large language models learn a strong natural language prior during pretraining, so they use the chain of thought much as humans use natural language.

context: A research group is considering how to establish whether chains-of-thought (the intermediate reasoning text produced by language models before an answer) are monitorable enough to be relied on for oversight. Existing practice leans on proxies such as faithfulness tests, in which a hint is injected into a prompt and the reasoning is checked for acknowledging it. Such proxies often label reasoning as unfaithful even when the text still carries useful information about what the model did. There is no agreed set of evaluations or metrics for monitorability. The group must decide what kind of evidence to put forward as the basis for judging whether chains-of-thought can be relied on.
a_text: Build an automatic detector that reads the chain-of-thought to judge whether an injected clue was used, and report its true-positive and specificity rates even on reasoning labeled unfaithful.
b_text: Recommend that developers and the research community prototype and converge on standardized monitorability evaluations and metrics in place of existing proxies.
reason: Faithfulness evaluations do not disambiguate propensity from necessity to externalize reasoning and only cover simple question answering, and it is unclear what level of monitorability is sufficient for safety.

context: A research team studies whether monitoring a language model's chain-of-thought (CoT) can reliably detect misbehavior. Existing evidence shows that CoT monitors often catch problematic reasoning in current models. However, this success has two possible explanations: the model may need to reason out loud to complete the task (necessity), or the model may simply tend to verbalize its reasoning even when it could do without (propensity). These explanations imply different things about how well monitoring will hold up when models are trained or incentivized to hide their reasoning. The team must decide how to handle this ambiguity in the existing evidence when presenting and building on it.
a_text: Separate necessity from propensity empirically by building tasks that require a chain of thought for success, then test whether the model can evade monitors when it must reason out loud.
b_text: Leave the interpretation open by stating that the split between necessity and propensity is unclear, and argue that monitoring stays useful for tasks that require a chain of thought.
reason: Future models may face incentives to hide reasoning that override natural propensity, but tasks hard enough to need CoT would still be monitorable.

context: A research team studying chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in language models found that the stated reasoning often fails to faithfully mention clues that influence the model's answers, so CoTs appear unreliable as explanations. However, they also found that a simple automatic detector flagged nearly all instances of clue use in the CoTs despite this apparent unfaithfulness. The team must decide how strongly to recommend investment in monitoring or scrutinizing CoTs relative to other safety research directions.
a_text: Recommend CoT monitoring only as an addition to existing safety research directions and not as a replacement for them.
b_text: Argue that CoT scrutiny is a highly promising avenue in its own right, rather than a supplement to other safety work.
reason: CoT monitoring cannot by itself give strong evidence of safety, may miss harms, may fail on more advanced models, and firm commitments to protect CoT may trade off against more effective interventions like process supervision.

context: A research team is building a monitoring setup to detect undesirable or unsafe behavior by an AI agent that reasons step by step before acting and then uses tools to complete tasks. The agent produces internal reasoning (chain of thought), tool calls and final outputs. The team must decide what the monitors, which flag suspicious behavior, are allowed to see. One consideration is that internal reasoning may reveal intent that actions alone do not. Another is that reasoning may be unfaithful, may be shaped by the monitoring itself, or may make results harder to compare with setups that observe only external behavior. The team must fix the monitors' input before running the evaluations.
a_text: Show monitors the agent's internal reasoning alongside its tool calls and outputs.
b_text: Hide the reasoning from monitors and limit them to tool calls and outputs.
reason: CoT can be illegible after RL, unfaithful, or absent in future models, so internal traces are assumed unavailable or untrustworthy

context: A research team is improving a prompt for a language model through human-guided refinement, in which a person reads outputs, edits the prompt, and checks whether results improve. The team must decide how long to keep refining. Early rounds produced visible gains, but it is unclear how much further manual iteration would help, and manual rounds are costly and hard to reproduce. The team can either end the process at a small fixed number of rounds, or change the procedure so that refinement continues under an explicit, recorded acceptance rule.
a_text: Automate the refinement, log every score, and accept a new prompt only when it beats the current one on a predefined metric.
b_text: Stop the human-guided refinement after a fixed small number of rounds, whatever the scores show at that point.
reason: Further targeted fixes became counterproductive, because fixing specific failure modes introduced new failures elsewhere without performance gains

context: A research team is building a detector that monitors the behavior of AI agents and flags malicious activity. To create a test set, they ran agents on tasks where each agent was assigned a hidden side task alongside its main task. Some of the resulting trajectories show the agent trying to carry out the side task but failing to complete it. The team must decide how these failed-side-task trajectories enter the evaluation. Their intent was malicious in every case, but the harmful outcome did not occur. The choice affects whether the test set measures detection of attempted malicious behavior or only of successful malicious behavior.
a_text: Remove the trajectories with failed side tasks from the test set and leave them unlabeled instead of counting them as attacks.
b_text: Keep the trajectories with failed side tasks in the test set and label them as positive attack attempts according to their assigned intent.
reason: Ascribing intent without ground-truth verification is unreliable, so only verified side-task successes are labeled positive

context: A research team is designing experiments in which language models act as monitors. They must decide which monitor models to include. Five candidate monitors are available: three established models and two of the newest, most capable frontier models. Including more monitors broadens coverage of monitor capability, but it also adds evaluation cost and complexity. The team must fix the monitor set before running the main experiments.
a_text: Expand the monitor set to all five models by adding the two newest frontier models to the three established ones.
b_text: Restrict the monitor set to the three established models and exclude the two newest frontier models.
reason: They were too costly

context: A research team is building an automated monitor, itself a language model, that reads transcripts of AI agent behavior and produces a suspicion score indicating whether a transcript should be flagged under a given monitoring instruction. The scores will be used to separate transcripts that warrant flagging from those that do not, by setting a decision threshold and evaluating detection performance. The team must decide the output format the monitor uses to express its score. The format affects how finely scores can rank transcripts, how many ties occur, and how flexibly thresholds can be tuned afterward.
a_text: Prompt the monitor to output a discrete integer suspicion score from 1 to 10 for each transcript, then set the flagging threshold on those integers.
b_text: Prompt the monitor to output a continuous probability between 0 and 1 that the transcript should be flagged, then set the flagging threshold on those probabilities.
reason: It significantly outperforms binary in the low-FPR regime, matches 5x-averaged binary at a fifth of the cost, and LLMs calibrate poorly over 100 points

context: A research team evaluated prompts across several task categories, including a threat-modeling category based on the STRIDE framework. A prompt-sweep stage produced results that were nearly saturated in every category, with little room left for improvement. The team then added a human refinement step, in which people manually revised the prompts. This step produced no meaningful improvement in most categories. It produced one statistically significant gain, on the STRIDE category. The team had to decide how to interpret this single gain against the otherwise saturated results, and what it implied for the claim that performance is saturated.
a_text: Treat the STRIDE gain as a real signal that threat modeling responds differently, conclude that saturation is not uniform, and run follow-up tests with more refined prompts before generalizing.
b_text: Treat the STRIDE gain as an isolated exception, conclude that performance is largely saturated at the prompt-sweep stage, and note that STRIDE may tolerate further optimization.
reason: The improvement is isolated

context: A research team studied automated prompt optimization for language models and found that heavy optimization, even with sophisticated search procedures, fails to outperform simply selecting the best prompt from a small set of simple candidates. The team must decide how to account for this result in their write-up. Several factors could plausibly contribute: the synthetic evaluation data may be narrow or contain artifacts that limit what prompts can influence, prompting may have fundamental limits as a lever for improving performance, or recent models may already have absorbed most of what prompt techniques once provided. The experiments did not isolate any one of these factors, so the evidence does not clearly favor one account over the others.
a_text: Commit to one explanation, that modern models already internalize what prompt tricks once unlocked, so prompts have little leverage and tuning yields small gains.
b_text: Present two competing explanations, narrow or artifact-heavy synthetic data and fundamental limits of prompting, as unresolved and propose future work to test each.
reason: The current evidence does not distinguish between the two

context: A research team is building and comparing monitors that flag harmful or undesirable behavior from an AI system, scoring each output with a suspicion score. They need a single primary metric to report and compare monitor performance across settings. In deployment, monitors can only be used if they produce very few false alarms on benign activity, since review capacity is limited and false alarms are costly. Scores can be computed on both benign and misbehaving examples, and a threshold can be chosen from benign data. The metric should reflect performance in the low false-positive regime rather than across all thresholds. Candidate choices differ in whether they summarize performance over a range of low false positive rates or at one specific operating point.
a_text: Adopt normalized partial area under the ROC curve over a restricted low false positive rate range as the primary monitor metric.
b_text: Adopt true positive rate at one fixed low false positive rate, with the threshold set on benign data, as the primary monitor metric.
reason: Standard AUROC includes the impractical high-FPR regime, while log-AUROC is sensitive to the threshold parameter epsilon and noisy at small sample sizes

context: A research team measured whether language models can tell evaluation transcripts apart from real-world deployment transcripts. Each model was shown a transcript and asked, through probe questions in a multiple-choice format, whether it came from an evaluation, and gave a probability. Calibration curves plotted against the diagonal show that models systematically assign higher evaluation probability than the true frequency warrants, so the curves fall below the diagonal. The team must decide how to interpret this over-classification of transcripts as evaluations. One candidate explanation is that it reflects the models' own learned priors about what evaluation transcripts look like. Another is that it comes from the measurement setup itself.
a_text: Interpret the below-diagonal curves as a real bias in the models' priors, where artificial or templated transcript features drive a miscalibrated evaluation base rate that a prior-shift correction could partly fix.
b_text: Interpret the below-diagonal curves as partly a measurement artifact, caused by probe questions priming models to consider evaluation and by instruction-tuned models' overconfidence on multiple-choice prompts.
reason: PQs introduce the possibility of evaluation, which may push models to consider transcripts evaluative; prior work notes similar overconfidence.

context: A research team evaluates language models on public benchmarks and finds that the models differ in how well they discriminate between items or outcomes on those benchmarks. One possible explanation is that the models have memorized the public benchmark content during training, so that apparent discriminative ability reflects exposure to the test material rather than genuine capability. The team has access to several models, including older and newer ones, and must decide how to address this memorization explanation in their analysis.
a_text: Measure memorization directly by testing how well each model reproduces benchmark text, and compare the results between older and newer models.
b_text: Acknowledge that memorization could plausibly contribute to the models' discriminative ability, without attempting to quantify its effect.
reason: Evaluation datasets derive from public benchmarks, but such occurrences are rare and hard to quantify.

context: A research team wants to study evaluation awareness in frontier language models, meaning whether models can tell that an interaction is a test rather than real deployment. They have access to a large pool of transcripts from many existing sources, covering both evaluation-style and real-world deployment-style interactions. They must decide what the central measured quantity of the study will be. One possibility is to measure how well models can label transcripts as coming from evaluation or deployment. Another is to measure whether model behavior changes when evaluation cues are present. Either study would use a set of about 1,000 items drawn from roughly 60 sources. The choice determines how the benchmark is built, what the primary metric is, and what the study can claim about models.
a_text: Frame the study around transcript classification, build a benchmark of transcripts labeled as evaluation or deployment, and use classification accuracy as measured by AUC as the primary metric.
b_text: Frame the study around behavioral change under perceived evaluation, build matched scenario pairs that vary only evaluation cues, and use the behavior shift between paired conditions as the primary metric.
reason: Evaluation awareness could compromise the reliability of evaluations, and no comprehensive test suite existed to measure it.

context: A research team measured language models' behavior on a set of questions and observed that some models produced meta-reasoning, remarking in their reasoning that the question itself implied they were being evaluated. This raised the issue of whether such awareness affects the measurements. The rate of spontaneous verbalized awareness was known to be only a lower bound for some models, such as a small reasoning model, because unverbalized awareness could not be observed. The team had to decide how to handle this meta-reasoning in their analysis and conclusions.
a_text: Decline to claim a causal effect of awareness and note that some models' evaluation awareness may be underestimated, so other measurement strategies may be needed.
b_text: Run a follow-up experiment that rephrases the questions to remove evaluation cues and compare the results with the original prompts to test directly whether awareness affects the measurements.
reason: Causal influence of the reasoning on final decisions has not been established.

context: A team is deciding which product area within AGI safety is the strongest candidate to pursue as a venture or focused program. context: A research team is designing experiments on intrinsification, where an agent's instrumental goal comes to be pursued as if it were the system goal (goal switching). The setting involves an agent with two competing goals: profit maximization and emission minimization. The team must decide which goal serves as the system goal assigned to the agent and which serves as the instrumental, competing goal that may displace it. The choice determines the direction in which goal switching is tested and how strongly the system goal is elicited in the prompts. Both pairings use the same two goals but reverse their roles.
a_text: Assign profit maximization as the system goal and emission minimization as the competing goal when testing goal switching.
b_text: Assign emission minimization as the system goal and profit maximization as the competing goal, using strong goal elicitation throughout.

context: A research team wants to study goal drift in autonomous language-model agents, meaning a gradual departure from an originally assigned objective over a long period of operation. Asking models whether they still hold their original goal is unreliable, because self-reports may not match actual behavior. The team therefore needs a measurement approach that infers drift from what the agent does rather than from what it says. Two designs are under consideration: one sets the agent in a concrete simulated setting where its choices are discrete, quantifiable actions that can be compared directly against the assigned goal; the other lets the agent pursue open-ended tasks and tracks how the mix of task categories it works on changes across time windows.
a_text: Use a simulated stock trading environment in which goal alignment is read directly from quantifiable actions such as buying and selling stocks.
b_text: Categorize the tasks the agent pursues in each time window and flag goal drift when the distribution of categories shifts significantly between two time points.
reason: Self-reports of LMs about their goals may be unfaithful; the environment also presents natural tensions between objectives and a realistic test bed.

context: A research team is building a simulated trading environment to study how AI agents behave when they pursue an instrumental goal that differs from the goal given in their system prompt. The evaluation phase of each run requires the agent to start with a portfolio concentrated in stocks aligned with the instrumental goal. In initial runs, the agents did not reliably reach such a portfolio before the evaluation phase began, and some converged to portfolios with substantial holdings outside the instrumental-goal-aligned stocks. a_text: Resample the instrumental goal pursuit trajectories by hand whenever an agent ends with a portfolio that is not sufficiently concentrated in instrumental-goal-aligned stocks.

context: A research team studied goal drift in language-model agents, where an agent gradually departs from its assigned objective during a long task. They hypothesised that drift is driven by pattern-matching, in which the agent imitates the behaviour in its preceding context instead of keeping to its original goal. To test this, they ran a random-sentence ablation and measured correlations between context features and drift. Most of these correlations were not statistically significant, though some trends pointed in the direction the hypothesis predicted. They also had drift measurements across several scenario types, including goal-switching scenarios that require the agent to adapt its behaviour and scenarios with purely adversarial pressure. The team had to decide which conclusion to draw and how strongly to state it in light of the mostly non-significant evidence.
a_text: Describe the random-sentence ablation results as only suggestive evidence for the pattern-matching hypothesis, given the mostly non-significant correlations.
b_text: Compare drift across scenario types and conclude that it arises mainly when the agent must adapt its behaviour, as in goal-switching, rather than under pure adversarial pressure.
reason: Despite stronger correlations, most of the correlations are not statistically significant.

context: A research team studied why a language model agent drifts away from its assigned goal over a long interaction history. Two competing explanations were under consideration: a goal-reasoning hypothesis, in which the model drifts because of how it reasons about the goal, and a pattern-matching hypothesis, in which the model imitates regularities in the preceding context. A third possibility, a token-distance hypothesis, held that drift arises simply from how far the goal sits from the current position in context. The team ran a cross-conditioning ablation that manipulated the goal-reasoning component and obtained results that were not clearly decisive. They had to decide how to proceed in interpreting this ablation.
a_text: Conclude that the ablation gives only limited support for goal reasoning, which plays a secondary role to pattern-matching.
b_text: Test the token-distance hypothesis by replacing the long interaction history with a single user message of repeated tokens matched in length.
reason: Individual differences are usually not statistically significant and substantial performance gaps persist between models in both conditions.

context: A research team studied why model behavior drifts over the course of a long generation. One hypothesis held that drift arises from the growing token distance between the original instructions and the current output position. To test it, the team ran ablations on token distance. In one ablation, the instrumental phase of the original setting was replaced with a repeated-token message, which changed the content while keeping the distance. In another, tokens were shuffled within windows of increasing size, which disrupted token position and local distance. The team had to decide how to interpret these ablation results with respect to the token distance hypothesis.
a_text: Probe the importance of token position and distance, by shuffling tokens within large windows and measuring the resulting small increase in perplexity.
b_text: Reject the token distance hypothesis, because replacing the instrumental phase with a repeated-token message produced much lower drift than the original setting.

context: A research team studies goal drift in language-model agents, where an agent that is switched from one goal to another during a task keeps following the earlier goal or pursues it instrumentally. context: A team is deploying a guardrail that screens the actions or outputs of an automated system and must decide whether it is reliable enough to trust. context: A research team studies how post-training choices such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) interact in language models. context: A research team is building a pipeline that uses a frontier language model as a teacher to generate rationales, which will then be used to train a smaller model. context: A research team is evaluating several prompted frontier language models as baselines on a task involving covert, goal-directed misaligned behavior (scheming). context: A research team is training a smaller language model, Qwen3-8B, by distilling data from a teacher model.
